entries.explanation: Matthew says Mary became pregnant through the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph came together. Christians connect this unusual birth with Genesis's reference to the woman's offspring.
The New Testament says Jesus came to destroy the devil's work. Christians identify that victory with the offspring who crushes the serpent in Genesis.
Acts describes Jesus being taken up into heaven. Christians treat Enoch's earlier disappearance into God's presence as a preview of that event.
Luke includes Shem in Jesus's genealogy. Christians combine that ancestry with the belief that Jesus is God incarnate.
Acts quotes the promise that every family will be blessed through Abraham's offspring, then presents Jesus as the one sent to bring that blessing.

passages.social_text: ‘Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed.’ When God raised up His Servant, He sent Him first to you to bless you.

entries.explanation: Paul explicitly interprets Abraham's promised offspring as Christ. Christians therefore read the Genesis promise as reaching its climax in Jesus.
Hebrews calls Jesus an eternal high priest in Melchizedek's order. Christians see the priest-king in Genesis as the pattern behind that claim.
Hebrews interprets Melchizedek's titles as king of righteousness and king of peace, then compares him with the Son of God.

passages.social_text: First, his name means ‘king of righteousness.’ Then also, ‘king of Salem’ means ‘king of peace.’ Like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.

entries.explanation: At the Last Supper Jesus gives bread and wine a meaning centred on his body and blood. Later Christians connect that meal with Melchizedek's bread and wine.

passages.social_text: Jesus took bread … saying, ‘Take and eat; this is My body.’ Then He took the cup … ‘This is My blood of the covenant.’

entries.explanation: Luke's genealogy places Jesus in the family line of Isaac and Abraham. Christians see that as locating Jesus inside the promised covenant family.
John calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away sin. Christians connect that title with the animal God provides in Isaac's place.
Paul says the promised offspring is Christ. Christians therefore understand the worldwide blessing promised through Abraham's offspring as fulfilled through Jesus.
Paul identifies Christ as Abraham's promised offspring. Christians read the promise renewed through Isaac as another stage in the same family line.
Jesus repeats the distinctive movement of Jacob's angels but says they will ascend and descend on the Son of Man. Christians see Jesus taking the central place in the vision.
Luke places Jesus in the family line of Jacob, Isaac and Abraham. Christians identify him as the representative descendant through whom the family blessing reaches the nations.
Paul says God's Son arrived when the time had fully come. Christians combine that statement with Jesus's Judahite ancestry and read it as the arrival anticipated in Genesis.
Luke includes Judah in Jesus's genealogy. Christians see that ancestry as meeting the tribal qualification in Jacob's blessing.
Jesus describes himself as the one God sent. A traditional Christian interpretation connects that wording with a disputed claim that Shiloh means ‘the one sent.’
John portrays Jewish leaders and institutions still functioning before Jesus's death. Christians use that setting to argue that the Messiah arrived before Judah lost its identity.

passages.social_text: The chief priests and Pharisees convened the Sanhedrin … ‘The Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.’

entries.explanation: Jesus says he will gather other sheep into one flock. Christians connect that international gathering with the peoples giving allegiance to Judah's ruler.
Jesus says, ‘Before Abraham was born, I am.’ Christians hear an echo of God's self-identification to Moses and take it as a claim to divine identity.
Peter compares Christ's blood with that of an unblemished lamb. Christians see the flawless Passover animal as a pattern for Jesus's sinless sacrifice.

passages.social_text: You were redeemed … with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.

entries.explanation: Paul says Christ's blood saves believers from God's wrath. Christians compare that rescue with the blood-marked houses spared during Passover.

passages.social_text: Since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him!

entries.explanation: Paul explicitly calls Christ ‘our Passover lamb.’ Christians therefore understand the Passover rite as a pattern fulfilled in Jesus's death.
John says the soldiers did not break Jesus's legs and then invokes Scripture about an unbroken bone. Christians see a deliberate Passover connection.

passages.social_text: They did not break His legs. Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken.’

entries.explanation: Matthew links Jesus's name with his mission to save, while Acts pictures him exalted at God's right hand. Christians connect both ideas with the LORD's salvation and power in Exodus.
Luke calls Jesus the Holy One, and Acts calls him God's holy servant. Christians connect those descriptions with the LORD's holiness in Exodus.

passages.social_text: The Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.

entries.explanation: Paul explicitly says that the spiritual rock accompanying Israel was Christ. Christians therefore read the water-giving rock as a pattern of Jesus.
Luke's hymn says God acts through Jesus to show mercy promised to Israel's ancestors. Christians connect that mercy with God's declaration to Moses.

passages.social_text: He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David … to show mercy to our fathers.

entries.explanation: Ephesians describes Christ's self-giving as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God. Christians connect that wording with the pleasing aroma of the burnt offering.
Jesus sends the healed man to a priest with the offering required by Moses, calling it a testimony. Some Christians connect this with the later report that many priests joined the faith.
Hebrews directly contrasts the annual high priest's entry with Christ entering a greater sanctuary by his own blood and securing lasting redemption.

passages.social_text: Christ came as high priest … He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.

entries.explanation: Hebrews explicitly compares the bodies burned outside the camp with Jesus suffering outside the city gate.
Jesus describes his covenant blood as poured out for forgiveness and his life as given for many. Christians read these sayings through Leviticus's link between blood, life and atonement.
First John says Jesus's blood cleanses from every sin. Christians see this as the fulfilment of the atoning role assigned to blood in Leviticus.
